'''''Primula vulgaris''''' is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Primulaceae]], [[native plant|native]] to [[Eurasia]].<ref name=flora>''Flora Europaea'': [http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Primula+&SPECIES_XREF=vulgaris&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= ''Primula vulgaris'']</ref><ref name=grin>{{GRIN | access-date = 14 December 2017}}</ref> The [[common name]] of this plant is '''primrose''',<ref name=nhm>Natural History Museum: [http://internt.nhm.ac.uk/jobj/java/runjava.jobj?java=ctol.CTOLServer&method=printNamePage&accountref=987&NAMEID=8335 ''Primula vulgaris''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090322145045/http://internt.nhm.ac.uk/jobj/java/runjava.jobj?java=ctol.CTOLServer&method=printNamePage&accountref=987&NAMEID=8335 |date=2009-03-22 }}</ref> or occasionally '''common primrose''' or '''English primrose''' to distinguish it from other ''[[Primula]]'' species referred to as primroses.

==Description==
''Primula vulgaris'' is a [[perennial]] growing {{convert|10|-|30|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} tall, with a basal rosette of [[leaves]] which are more-or-less [[evergreen]] in favoured habitats. The leaves are {{Convert|5–25|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long and {{Convert|2–6|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} broad, often heavily wrinkled, with an irregularly [[crenate]] to dentate margin. The leaf blade is gradually attenuated towards the base and unevenly toothed. The single stem, extremely short, is hidden in the centre of the leaf [[rosette (botany)|rosette]].<ref name=":0">Manfred A. Fischer, Karl Oswald, Wolfgang Adler: Excursion flora for Austria, Liechtenstein and South Tyrol . 3rd, improved edition. Upper Austria, Biology Center of the Upper Austrian Provincial Museums, Linz 2008, {{ISBN|978-3-85474-187-9}} , p.  685 .</ref>

Blooming in early spring in the [[Northern Hemisphere]] (February–April), the delicately scented [[flower]]s are 2–4 cm in diameter, borne singly on short slender stems.<ref name=":0" /> They are typically pale yellow, though white or pink forms are often seen in nature. The flowers are [[actinomorphic]] with a superior ovary which later forms a [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] opening by valves to release the small black seeds. The flowers are [[plant sexuality|hermaphrodite]] but [[heterostylous]]; individual plants bear either ''pin'' flowers ([[longuistylous]] flower: with the capita of the [[carpel|style]] prominent) or ''thrum'' flowers ([[brevistylous]] flower: with the [[stamen]]s prominent). [[Fertilisation]] can only take place between pin and thrum flowers. Pin-to-pin and thrum-to-thrum [[pollination]] is ineffective.<ref name="blamey">Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}</ref><ref name="rhs">Huxley, A, ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
===Subspecies===
[[Image:Primula, from Riza DSC071156565.JPG|thumb|''Primula vulgaris'' subsp. ''sibthorpii'']]

Three [[subspecies]] are accepted by some sources:<ref name=flora/><ref name=rhs/>
*''Primula vulgaris'' subsp. ''vulgaris''. Western and southern Europe. As described above; flowers pale yellow.
*''Primula vulgaris'' subsp. ''balearica'' <small>(Willk.) W.W.Sm. & Forrest</small>. [[Balearic Islands]] ([[endemic (ecology)|endemic]]). Flowers white. Leaf stem longer than leaf blade.
*''Primula vulgaris'' subsp. ''sibthorpii'' <small>(Hoffmanns.) W.W.Sm. & Forrest</small>. Balkans, southwest Asia. Flowers pink to red or purple.
[[Plants of the World Online]] accepts only one subspecies in addition to the nominate subsp. ''vulgaris'':<ref name=POWO_702779-1/>
*''Primula vulgaris'' subsp. ''atlantica'' <small>(Maire & Wilczek) Greuter & Burdet</small>. Morocco to Algeria.

The primrose is distinguished from other species of ''Primula'' by its pale yellow (in the nominate subspecies) flowers produced singly on long flower stalks which are covered in rather shaggy hairs. The flowers open flat rather than concave as in the case of ''[[Primula veris]]'', the cowslip.

A pink form is widely seen, growing amongst the much more common yellow forms; this may be a genetic variant rather than a garden escape.<ref>Mabey, Richard: ''Flora britannica'' (Chatto & Windus, 1996). {{ISBN|1856193772}}</ref><ref name=Clapham>Clapham, A., Tutin, T., & Warburg, E. (1962). ''Flora of the Brish Isles''.</ref> Occasional red forms are more likely to be [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] from garden varieties.<ref name=blamey/>

===Etymology===
The [[scientific name]] ''Primula'' is a diminutive of the [[Latin language|Latin]] {{wikt-lang|la|primus}} {{gloss|prime}}, alluding to the fact that this flower is among the first to appear in spring.<ref>François Couplan, Eva Styner, Guide to Wild Edible and Toxic Plants , Delachaux and Niestlé, coll. "The guides of the naturalist" ( {{ISBN|2-603-00952-4}} )</ref> The [[vernacular]] name has the same meaning: primrose derives from a [[late Latin]] form {{lang|la|prima rosa}}, consisting of {{lang|la|prima}} {{gloss|first}} (feminine), and {{lang|la|rosa}} {{gloss|rose}}.<ref>{{OEtymD|primrose}}</ref>

The Latin [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] {{wikt-lang|la|vulgaris}} means "common", in the sense of "widespread".<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book | last=Harrison |first=Lorraine | title=RHS Latin for Gardeners | year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley | location=United Kingdom | isbn=978-1845337315 }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The native range of ''P. vulgaris'' encompasses [[Western Europe|western]] and [[southern Europe]]. In the north, the distribution area extends from [[central Norway]] near the [[Faroe Islands]] via the [[British Isles]], [[Denmark]], [[northern Germany]], the [[Netherlands]], [[Belgium]] and [[France]] to southern [[Portugal]] in the south and the tip of North Africa in [[Algeria]]. To the east, the range extends through the southern European peninsulas to the [[Crimea]], [[Balkans]], [[Syria]], [[Turkey]], and [[Armenia]].

In appropriate conditions, ''P. vulgaris'' can cover the ground in open woods and shaded hedgerows. It is found mainly by streams, under bushes, in orchards and clear, moist deciduous forests. Occasionally it also appears in meadows. In Central Europe plants thrive best on nutrient-rich, but lime-poor, humus-rich, loose and often stony loam soils in winter-mild situations. In more populated areas it has sometimes suffered from over-collection and theft so that few natural displays of primroses in abundance can now be found. However it is common on motorway verges and railway embankments where human intervention is restricted. To prevent excessive damage to the species, picking of primroses or the removal of primrose plants from the wild is illegal in many countries, e.g. the UK [[Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981]].<ref>Section 13, part 1b.</ref>

==Ecology==
===Pollinators===
Most (90%) individuals are heterostylous, the minority monostylous. The flowers of the species are visited by a variety of insects, including butterflies ([[Lepidoptera]]), [[Hymenoptera]], beetles ([[Coleoptera]]) and [[Diptera]]. Which visitors pollinate plants is not fully established. However, good pollinators are said to be [[bumblebees]] and hairy flies of the genus ''[[Bombylius]]''. However, the most common visitors to the flowers are small beetles of the genus ''[[Meligethes]]'' – often there are up to 12 or more [[pollen]]-covered individuals in a single flower. The beetles also fly from flower to flower and, at least theoretically, are well suited as pollinators.<ref name="bioflora">{{cite journal | vauthors=((Jacquemyn, H.)), ((Endels, P.)), ((Brys, R.)), ((Hermy, M.)), ((Woodell, S. R. J.)) | journal=Journal of Ecology | title=Biological Flora of the British Isles: ''Primula vulgaris'' Huds. (P. acaulis (L.) Hill) | volume=97 | issue=4 | pages=812–833 | date= 2009 | issn=1365-2745 | doi=10.1111/j.1365-2745.2009.01513.x}}</ref><ref>Dietmar Aichele, Heinz-Werner Schwegler: The flowering plants of Central Europe , Franckh-Kosmos-Verlag, 2nd revised edition 1994, 2000, Volume 3, {{ISBN|3-440-08048-X}}</ref>

===Seed dispersal===
The seeds have an [[elaiosome]] and are spread by ants ([[myrmecochory]]). Small mammals also feed on and transport the seeds.<ref name = "bioflora"></ref>

===Herbivores and pathogens===
Numerous invertebrate herbivores in the orders [[Diptera]] and [[Lepidoptera]] feed on the leaves of ''P. vulgaris'', including multiple moth species in the genera ''[[Noctua (moth)|Noctua]]'' and ''[[Xestia]]''.<ref name="bioflora"></ref>

Several pathogenic [[fungi]] and [[oomycete]]s infect the leaves of ''P. vulgaris'', including the [[rust fungus]] ''[[Puccinia primulae]]'' and the [[downy mildew]] ''[[Peronospora oerteliana]]''. The [[smut fungus]] ''[[Urocystis primulae]]'' infects the flowers.<ref>{{Citation | vauthors=((Ellis, W. N.)) | year=2001 | title=Primula acaulis | url=https://bladmineerders.nl/en/host-plants/plantae/spermatopsida/angiosperma/eudicots/superasterids/asterids/ericales/primulaceae/primuloideae/primula/primula-acaulis/ | access-date=16 February 2026}}</ref><ref name = "bioflora"></ref>

Primrose flowers, and the flowers of related members of the Primulaceae, are often removed from their stalks and scattered on the ground by [[Eurasian bullfinch|bullfinch]]es apparently consuming the ovaries and nectaries.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Darwin |first=Charles |date=1874 |title=Flowers of the Primrose destroyed by Birds |journal=Nature |volume=9 |page=482 |bibcode=1874Natur...9Q.482D |doi=10.1038/009482a0 |doi-access=free |number=482}}</ref><ref name = "bioflora"></ref> [[Common pheasant|Pheasant]]s, [[Old World sparrow|sparrow]]s, and [[European fallow deer|fallow]] and [[Reeves's muntjac|muntjac]] deer are also known to eat the flowers. Small mammals both feed on and transport the seeds.<ref name = "bioflora"></ref>

==Cultivation==
The wild primrose is a staple of [[cottage garden]] plantings, and is widely available as seeds or young plants.  It grows best in moist but well-drained soil in light shade. It is increased by seed and [[division (horticulture)|division]]. The throat is usually coloured rich yellow.

Primrose breeding of named coloured varieties became popular in the nineteenth and early twentieth century.<ref>{{cite web|title=Primrose-tinted spectacles|url=http://www.irishtimes.com/life-and-style/homes-and-property/2.770/primrose-tinted-spectacles-1.571142|publisher=Irish Times}}</ref> Numerous [[cultivar]]s have been selected for [[garden]] planting, often derived from subsp. ''sibthorpii'' or [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] between the subspecies; these and other garden hybrids are available in a wide range of colours, including white, yellow and red, or brown and red in all gradations as well as dark red, pink, purple, dark brown and dark blue, and with an extended flowering season.<ref name=rhs/>

The term ''Polyanthus'', or ''[[Primula × polyantha]]'', refers to various tall-stemmed and multi-coloured strains of ''P. vulgaris'' × ''[[Primula veris|P. veris]]'' [[hybrid (biology)#In plants|hybrids]]. Though perennial, they may be short-lived and are typically grown from seed or from young plants as [[biennial plant|biennials]].

==Uses==
Both flowers and leaves are edible, the flavour ranging between mild lettuce and more bitter salad greens. The leaves can be cooked in soup but preferably with other plants because they are sometimes a little strong. The leaves can also be used for tea, and the young flowers can be made into primrose wine. In the past the whole plant and especially the root were considered to have [[analgesic]], anti-[[spasmodic]], [[diuretic]] and expectorant properties. It contains small amounts of [[saponin]]s, and was given for colds.<ref>SRJ Woodell: Natural Hybridization in Britain between Primula vulgaris Huds. (the primrose) and P. elatior (L.) Hill (the oxlip) . In: Watsonia . Volume  7 , No.  3 , 1969, pp.  115-127</ref>
''P. vulgaris'' foliage contains significant amounts of vitamin C.<ref>The Cambridge World History of Food, Volume One.</ref>

==In culture==

The primrose was [[Benjamin Disraeli]]'s favourite flower; [[Primrose Day]] and the [[Primrose League]] were given their names in honour of this.

Primroses also appear as a [[charge (heraldry)|charge]] in [[heraldry]], for example the coat of arms of the [[Earl of Rosebery]].

Italy chose a fuchsia primrose as the symbol of its 2020 [[COVID-19 vaccine|COVID-19 vaccination]] campaign.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Horowitz|first=Jason|date=2020-12-28|title=Italy Turns to Flower Power to Help Spread Vaccine Message|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/28/world/europe/italy-coronavirus-vaccine-flowers.html|access-date=2020-12-28|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

The primrose is on one side of Austria's [[5 euro cent coin]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Austria |url=https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/euro/euro-coins-and-notes/euro-coins/national-sides-euro-coins/austria_en |access-date=3 August 2022 |website=[[European Commission]]}}</ref>

Primrose Yellow exists in some paint and color systems and is named after this flower.<ref>{{Cite web |title=PANTONE 13-0755 TCX Primrose Yellow |url=https://www.pantone.com/connect/13-0755-TCX |access-date=30 September 2022 |website=[[Pantone]]}}</ref>

The primrose occurs frequently in [[Romantic poetry]], and has been celebrated, among others, by poets such as [[John Keats|Keats]], [[William Wordsworth|Wordsworth]], [[Oscar Wilde|Wilde]], [[Oliver Goldsmith|Goldsmith]] and [[Geoffrey Chaucer|Chaucer]]. <ref>{{Cite web |title=Famous Primrose Poems {{!}} Examples of Famous Primrose Poetry |url=https://www.poetrysoup.com/famous/poems/primrose |access-date=2024-04-29 |website=PoetrySoup.com |language=en}}</ref> In common parlance, the phrase "the primrose path" implies the thoughtless pursuit of pleasure, especially when it is seen to bring disastrous consequences. The original allusion is a reference in [[Shakespeare]]'s [[Hamlet]] (1.3.48-52) to "the primrose path of dalliance".<ref>{{Cite web |title=primrose |url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803100345831 |access-date=2024-05-02 |website=Oxford Reference |language=en }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Shakespeare Quick Quotes |url=https://www.shakespeare-online.com/quickquotes/quickquotehamletprimrose.html |website=Shakespeare Online |date=January 21, 2022}}</ref>

The old Roman name of the Primrose was Paralisos, that of the son of [[Priapus]] and [[Flora (mythology)|Flora]], who died of grief for the loss of his betrothed Melicerta, but was, by his parents, metamorphosed into the flower.<ref>[[Henry Irving|John Henry Brodribb]], Flowers and Plants for Designers and Schools, p. 49.</ref>

[[Primrose Everdeen]] from [[The Hunger Games|the Hunger Games]] is named after this plant.
